issues.legal_issue: Compensation for mental agony is not recoverable for an ordinary breach of a scheme-allotment contract when no capricious or mala fide exercise of administrative power is established.
material_facts: The development authority delayed or failed to provide the promised plot or flat under its scheme.
The Commission awarded compensation for the claimants’ mental agony arising from that failure.
No case of mala fide or capricious exercise of discretion was pleaded or established, and the Commission made no such finding.
issues.conclusion: The award of compensation for mental agony was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Contract Act and the Specific Relief Act, contractual damages generally compensate loss directly flowing from the breach and within the parties’ contemplation; ordinary contractual damages do not include injury to feelings or mental distress. Chitty on Contracts states a limited exception for contracts intended to provide peace of mind or where qualifying harm was contemplated. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994) 1 SCC 243 concerned compensation under administrative-law principles for proved capricious exercise of power; that basis was not established here.

rule.if: scheme_performance_dispute and ordinary_contract_breach and mental_agony_claim and not proven_capricious_abuse

predicates.scheme_performance_dispute: A claim arises from a public development authority’s scheme for allotting land or housing.
predicates.ordinary_contract_breach: The authority failed or unreasonably delayed performance of its contractual promise under the scheme.
predicates.mental_agony_claim: The claimant sought compensation for mental distress caused by the authority’s failure or delay.
predicates.proven_capricious_abuse: The claimant established a capricious or mala fide exercise of administrative power as the basis for compensation.
predicates.mental_agony_compensation_unavailable: Compensation for mental agony is not awarded for the ordinary contractual breach.

issues.definition: When a scheme-performance dispute involves an ordinary contractual breach and a claim for mental-agony compensation, but no capricious administrative abuse is established, that compensation is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: Interest may be awarded on equitable grounds on money refundable by a development authority even where no contractual promise or specifically applicable statutory provision requires payment of interest.
material_facts: The claimants had paid or deposited money under the authority’s schemes.
The authority was found responsible for unreasonable delay or failure to perform its promises, and the claimants were entitled to refunds.
The relevant contracts and correspondence contained no express or implied promise to pay interest, and no specifically applicable statutory provision authorising interest was identified.
issues.conclusion: The authority was not justified in resisting payment of interest on the amounts refundable to the claimants.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not itself apply to proceedings under the consumer legislation unless made applicable, but equitable principles may support an interest award in an appropriate case. Sovintorg (India) Ltd. v. State Bank of India, New Delhi (1999) 6 SCC 406 recognised that interest may be awarded on equitable grounds, including in lieu of compensation or damages. The Court applied those principles where the authority was at fault and the claimants were deprived of the use of their money.

rule.if: development_authority_refund_claim and refund_due and authority_fault and no_interest_promise

predicates.development_authority_refund_claim: A claimant seeks repayment of money paid or deposited under a public development authority’s scheme.
predicates.refund_due: The claimant is entitled to repayment of the deposited money.
predicates.authority_fault: The authority’s unreasonable delay or failure to perform caused the circumstances requiring repayment.
predicates.no_interest_promise: The parties made no express or implied promise to pay interest on the refundable money.
predicates.equitable_interest_awarded: Interest may be awarded on the refundable money on equitable grounds.

issues.definition: Where a claimant is owed a refund because of the authority’s fault and there was no promise to pay interest, equitable interest may be awarded.

issues.legal_issue: The rate of interest on a refund owed by a development authority must be assessed equitably in light of the circumstances and evidence of the case.
material_facts: The challenged orders in most of the appeals awarded interest at a higher rate.
The parties had tendered no evidence enabling the Court to determine an ideal rate for these cases.
The Court considered a lower rate just and proper in the circumstances, noting that the higher rate in Sovintorg had been influenced by the claimant’s particular financial difficulties.
issues.conclusion: The interest rate was reduced to a rate the Court considered just and proper for these cases.
issues.legal_principle: Sovintorg (India) Ltd. v. State Bank of India, New Delhi (1999) 6 SCC 406 does not establish a universally applicable interest rate; the rate depends on the circumstances of each case. Equitable interest should be neither too high nor too low, and the Court selected a just and proper rate where the parties had supplied no evidence supporting an ideal rate.

predicates.development_authority_refund_claim: A claimant seeks repayment of money paid or deposited under a public development authority’s scheme.
predicates.equitable_interest_awarded: Interest is awarded on the refundable money on equitable grounds.
predicates.no_rate_evidence: The parties provide no evidence enabling the court to identify an ideal rate of interest.
predicates.interest_rate_set_at_just_and_proper_lev: The court sets the interest rate at a level it considers just and proper in the circumstances.

issues.definition: When equitable interest is awarded on a development-authority refund claim and the parties provide no evidence of an ideal rate, the court sets a rate it considers just and proper.

issues.legal_issue: A scheme brochure’s no-interest term for a refund following surrender does not bar interest when the development authority’s own fault created the circumstances requiring the refund.
material_facts: The brochure stated that no interest would be payable if an applicant withdrew or surrendered the offer.
The authority was found responsible for the delay or failure that led to the claimants seeking refunds.
The claimants were therefore not themselves responsible for creating the circumstances that occasioned the refunds.
issues.conclusion: The no-interest term applied only where the claimant was responsible for creating the circumstances requiring a refund and did not prevent interest in these cases.
issues.legal_principle: The brochure term must be construed according to the circumstances it addresses: it applies when the claimant creates the occasion for repayment, not when the authority’s own fault makes repayment due. In that latter situation, the authority has no justification for resisting equitable interest.

predicates.development_authority_refund_claim: A claimant seeks repayment of money paid or deposited under a public development authority’s scheme.
predicates.brochure_disclaims_interest: The scheme brochure states that interest will not be paid on a refund following withdrawal or surrender.
predicates.authority_fault_caused_refund: The authority’s own fault created the circumstances requiring repayment.
predicates.brochure_term_does_not_bar_interest: The brochure’s no-interest term does not prevent an interest award.

issues.definition: When the brochure disclaims interest but the authority’s fault caused the refund, the disclaimer does not bar interest.
